questions.subtopic: Governance Versus Management. Board Oversight in Practice
questions.question: A shipping company's board receives detailed monthly IT reports, yet its minutes show no IT decisions, questions or follow-up actions in two years. Which conclusion is MOST appropriate for the IS auditor to draw?

options.A: The board is informed about IT but is not governing it
options.B: IT performed well, so no board decisions were needed
options.C: The reports are too technical for directors to act on
options.D: The board has formally delegated IT accountability to management

questions.key_concept: A board governs IT only when it sets direction and challenges results; receiving reports alone is not oversight.
questions.pre_read: Look at what the board does with information, not how much information it receives.
questions.correct_explanation: Governance means evaluating, directing and monitoring. Two years of reports with no decisions, questions or follow-up show the board receiving information without exercising any of those roles, so IT is in effect steering itself. Good performance does not explain the silence: even when results are on target, a governing board still sets direction, approves priorities and challenges what it is told. Passive receipt of reports is information, not oversight.

wrong_explanations.B: Even strong results need a board that sets direction and challenges reports. Two years without a single question cannot be explained by performance alone.
wrong_explanations.C: Hard-to-read reports can dull engagement. But nothing in the facts faults the reports, and two years without one question describes how the board behaves, not how the reports are written.
wrong_explanations.D: Nothing shows a formal delegation, and accountability for IT cannot be delegated anyway; the board keeps it whatever it hands to management.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because C faults report design that nothing in the facts questions, and D claims a delegation of accountability that a board cannot make.
Final two: A beats B because governing means directing and challenging, which good results do not replace; B mistakes silence for oversight.
Exam cue: reports that are received but never questioned or acted on point to information, not governance.

questions.subtopic: Managing IT People. Key-Person Dependency
questions.question: After two unplanned resignations stalled IT services, management wants to reduce the organization's dependence on individual staff. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Cross-train backups for the most senior engineer in each team
options.B: Offer retention bonuses to staff in hard-to-fill technical roles
options.C: Write detailed procedures for every system the IT function runs
options.D: Identify the roles and people that critical services rely on

questions.key_concept: Reducing key-person risk starts by identifying the roles critical services depend on; remedies follow that analysis.
questions.pre_read: For a FIRST question, ask what must be known before any remedy can be aimed.
questions.correct_explanation: Reducing dependence starts with knowing where it lies: which roles and individuals critical services cannot run without. That analysis directs cross-training, documentation and succession planning to the right places. Cross-training senior engineers acts before that analysis and assumes seniority equals criticality, yet the person a service depends on may be a junior specialist. Once key roles are known, cross-training them becomes the main remedy.

wrong_explanations.A: Seniority is not the same as criticality. Without first identifying key roles, backups may be trained for the wrong people.
wrong_explanations.B: Bonuses may keep people longer, but services still depend on them; illness or a later resignation leaves the same gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Documenting everything at once spreads effort thinly and still leaves no trained backup for the systems that matter most.

tips: Eliminate: B keeps the dependency in place, and C spreads effort across every system without creating a trained backup.
Final two: D beats A because cross-training works only once the critical roles are known; seniority is a poor guide to criticality.
Exam cue: for a FIRST question on people risk, identify key roles and single points of knowledge before choosing remedies.

questions.subtopic: Retention and Disposal. Former Customer Data
questions.question: A retailer's marketing team wants to keep former customers' identifiable purchase histories indefinitely for trend analysis, beyond their documented retention period. Which approach should the IS auditor recommend as MOST appropriate?

options.A: Ask former customers to consent to keeping their histories
options.B: Keep the histories, since trend analysis is a legitimate business purpose
options.C: Anonymize the histories once their retention period ends
options.D: Delete each customer's history as soon as the customer leaves

questions.key_concept: At the end of retention, data is deleted or made anonymous; anonymous data can still serve analysis without identifying anyone.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the stated purpose actually needs to know who each person is.
questions.correct_explanation: Trend analysis needs patterns, not identities. Anonymizing the histories when the retention period ends honors the schedule, because data that can no longer identify anyone is no longer personal data, while still giving marketing what it needs. Seeking consent from former customers is a weaker route: few will reply, consent can be withdrawn, and it keeps identifiable data indefinitely for a purpose that does not require it.

wrong_explanations.A: Consent is a valid lawful basis, but a lawful basis does not answer minimization: keep the least identifying form that still serves the purpose.
wrong_explanations.B: A legitimate purpose does not justify keeping identifiable data indefinitely when the purpose can be met without identities.
wrong_explanations.D: Deleting at departure ignores the documented retention period, which may exist for tax, warranty or dispute needs.

tips: Eliminate: B lets a business purpose override the retention period, and D destroys records before their documented period ends.
Final two: C beats A because the analysis does not need identities, so anonymizing meets it without chasing consent from people who left.
Exam cue: when a purpose needs patterns rather than people, anonymize at the end of retention instead of keeping identifiable data.
questions.framework_ref: GDPR Article 5(1)(e) (Storage Limitation); ISO/IEC 27002:2022 Control 8.11 (Data Masking); COBIT 2019 APO14.09 (Support data archiving and retention); GDPR Recital 26 (Anonymous information)

questions.subtopic: How Outside Rules Shape IT Governance. Cost of Compliance
questions.question: A software firm's management proposes not complying with a new law requiring breach reports within 72 hours, because expected fines would cost less than compliance. Which response should the IS auditor recommend as MOST appropriate?

options.A: Have the board accept the risk of noncompliance
options.B: Comply with the law in the most cost-effective way
options.C: Delay compliance until the regulator issues guidance
options.D: Have the IS audit team run breach reporting to save cost

questions.key_concept: Mandatory legal obligations are not open to cost trade-offs; management chooses how to comply, not whether to comply.
questions.pre_read: Sort the options into ways of complying and ways of not complying before weighing costs.
questions.correct_explanation: A legal duty is not a risk to buy out with a fine: management decides how to comply, not whether. The appropriate response is to meet the 72-hour requirement in the most cost-effective way. Board acceptance looks like proper risk governance, but no level of the organization can accept deliberately breaking the law, and fines often bring regulatory orders and reputational damage on top.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk acceptance covers risks within appetite, not deliberate breaches of law. Board approval would make the violation a board decision, not a lawful one.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for guidance can seem prudent with a new law. But the 72-hour duty is already in force, so delaying is still noncompliance the firm has chosen.
wrong_explanations.D: Running an operational process would impair the IS audit team's independence when it later audits breach reporting.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because C postpones a duty already in force, and D puts the IS auditors in charge of a process they must audit.
Final two: B beats A because no one, not even the board, can accept a deliberate breach of law as a risk decision.
Exam cue: for mandatory obligations, choose the answer about how to comply cost-effectively, never whether to comply.

questions.subtopic: Due Diligence, Contracts and SLAs. Source Code Escrow
questions.question: A hospital plans to run patient scheduling on a start-up's software as a service (SaaS) platform, relying on a source code escrow agreement if the start-up fails. What should be the IS auditor's PRIMARY concern?

options.A: Released code alone could not quickly restore the hosted service
options.B: The escrow agent might not confirm that deposits are complete
options.C: The escrow release triggers might not cover a service shutdown
options.D: Escrow could expose the start-up's code to its competitors

questions.key_concept: Source code escrow helps only customers able to run the code; hosted services need data return and service transition terms.
questions.pre_read: Picture the day after the start-up fails: what would the hospital actually need to keep scheduling patients?
questions.correct_explanation: Source code escrow protects a customer that can run the software itself. For a SaaS platform, the hospital has no hosting environment, operating staff or current copy of its data, so released code would not restore scheduling for weeks. Continuity needs data return and service transition terms. Deposit verification matters, but even a complete, verified deposit leaves the same gap, so it is a secondary concern.

wrong_explanations.B: Fit comes before execution. Deposit verification is a normal escrow term, yet refining a protection cannot cure a mismatch with the delivery model.
wrong_explanations.C: Clear triggers matter, but even a timely release would give the hospital code it has no infrastructure or staff to run.
wrong_explanations.D: Escrow agents hold deposits in confidence and release them only to the customer when agreed conditions occur, such as vendor failure.

tips: Eliminate: C refines release terms that still deliver only code, and D misreads escrow, which releases code only to the customer on agreed triggers.
Final two: A beats B because even a verified deposit cannot run a hosted service without infrastructure, data and operating staff.
Exam cue: match the protection to the delivery model; for hosted services, look for data return and service transition, not code alone.

questions.subtopic: IT Due Diligence in Mergers and Acquisitions. Ranking Deal Findings
questions.question: During due diligence on a software company whose revenue depends on one platform, an IS auditor records four findings. Which poses the GREATEST risk to the buyer's deal?

options.A: Two senior developers hold undocumented knowledge of the platform
options.B: The platform's core component license ends if the company is sold
options.C: The company runs an ERP version the buyer does not support
options.D: Several security policies have not been reviewed in over two years

questions.key_concept: Change-of-control clauses can end licenses or contracts a target depends on, so due diligence flags them before closing.
questions.pre_read: Ask which finding could stop the buyer from using what it is paying for, and which can be managed later.
questions.correct_explanation: A change-of-control clause that ends the core component license threatens the buyer's right to run the platform that produces all the revenue. Only terms agreed before closing, such as the licensor's consent or a price change, can address it. Undocumented developer knowledge is a serious key-person risk, but retention agreements and documentation can reduce it, while the clause lets the licensor end or reprice the right to run the revenue platform.

wrong_explanations.A: An auditor would flag key-person dependency in any software deal, yet risks the buyer controls after closing usually rank below those a third party holds.
wrong_explanations.C: Unsupported ERP versions add integration cost, which buyers notice. It is a post-closing integration task, and it does not threaten the right to run the platform that earns the revenue.
wrong_explanations.D: Overdue policy reviews are a minor governance gap the buyer can fix after closing, with little effect on the price or the deal.

tips: Eliminate: C is a routine integration task after closing, and D is a minor policy gap the buyer can fix later.
Final two: B beats A because the licensor could end or reprice the right to run the revenue platform, while key-person risk can be reduced with retention terms.
Exam cue: in due diligence, rank findings by whether they threaten what the buyer is paying for; change-of-control clauses often do.

questions.subtopic: Governing Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technology. AI in Purchased Systems
questions.question: A city government's departments have enabled artificial intelligence (AI) features in several purchased systems that serve residents, but no one knows how many exist. What should the IS auditor recommend FIRST?

options.A: Build an inventory of AI uses, each rated by its impact
options.B: Test each AI feature found so far for biased outcomes
options.C: Ask each vendor to certify that its AI features are fair
options.D: Disable the AI features until a council policy is approved

questions.key_concept: AI governance starts with an inventory of every AI use, including vendor and embedded features, ranked by impact.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the city must know before it can decide which AI features to assess, test or switch off.
questions.correct_explanation: Governance starts with knowing what exists. An inventory of AI uses, with an owner and an impact rating for each, shows which features affect residents most and where assessment and monitoring must go first. Testing features for bias is valuable, but testing only those found so far, without an inventory, leaves unknown high-impact uses untested and gives no basis for ranking the effort.

wrong_explanations.B: Bias testing is a core AI assurance step, but every test is scoped from a known population.
wrong_explanations.C: The city stays accountable for decisions made with vendor AI. A vendor's self-certification is not independent evidence of fair outcomes.
wrong_explanations.D: Disabling the features could halt services to residents before anyone knows which ones are low risk. It is a disproportionate first response.

tips: Eliminate: C hands assurance to vendors although the city stays accountable, and D halts services before knowing which features matter.
Final two: A beats B because testing cannot be targeted or complete until an inventory shows which AI uses exist and which matter most.
Exam cue: when no one knows what exists, the first step is an inventory ranked by risk; assessment and testing follow.

questions.subtopic: Capability and Maturity Models. Self-Assessed Ratings
questions.question: Process owners rated the incident management process at capability level 4 in a self-assessment, but the IS auditor finds no one collects data on how it performs. What is the MOST LIKELY conclusion?

options.A: The rating stands, because process owners know the process best
options.B: The rating is overstated, as quantitative measurement is absent
options.C: The rating stands, since practices are documented and followed
options.D: No conclusion is possible until an external assessor repeats the rating

questions.key_concept: Capability ratings must rest on evidence; level 4 requires quantitative measurement, so a rating without performance data is overstated.
questions.pre_read: Recall what separates level 4 from level 3, then check whether the evidence meets it.
questions.correct_explanation: Level 4 means the process is measured and controlled with quantitative data. If no one collects performance data, that criterion cannot be met, so the self-assessed rating is most likely overstated, and the IS auditor reports it. An independent reassessment could confirm the true level, but the evidence already contradicts level 4, so the conclusion does not have to wait for one.

wrong_explanations.A: Owners rating their own processes tend to be optimistic. A rating must rest on evidence, and here the evidence contradicts it.
wrong_explanations.C: Documented, consistent practice describes level 3. Level 4 also needs performance measured and controlled with data.
wrong_explanations.D: The missing performance data already fails the level 4 criterion. A reassessment may set the exact level, but the overstatement is clear now.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a self-rating the evidence contradicts, and C mistakes level 3 practice for level 4.
Final two: B beats D because the missing data already fails the level 4 criterion, so the IS auditor can conclude without waiting.
Exam cue: know what each capability level requires; level 4 means measured, data-driven control, and level 5 adds continual improvement.

questions.subtopic: Privacy by Design and by Default. Readmission Analytics
questions.question: A European hospital's analysts must follow each patient across visits to study readmissions, but never need names or contact details. Which design should the IS auditor recommend as BEST?

options.A: Replace identifiers with codes, holding the linking key separately
options.B: Encrypt the full records and give analysts the decryption key
options.C: Give analysts full records under signed confidentiality agreements
options.D: Remove names, using the hospital record number to link visits

questions.key_concept: Privacy by design minimizes exposure: pseudonymization supports linked analysis, while a separately protected key limits re-identification risk.
questions.pre_read: List what the analysts actually need, then find the option that gives them that and nothing more.
questions.correct_explanation: Pseudonymization gives analysts what they need, a consistent code linking each patient's visits, without identities. Because the key linking codes to patients is held separately under its own access control, analysts cannot readily re-identify patients, although the coded data remains personal data under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). Removing names looks similar, but the hospital record number is itself an identifier that many staff can look up, so patients remain easily identifiable.

wrong_explanations.B: Encryption protects data in storage, but analysts holding the key see every identity. It does not reduce the personal data they are exposed to.
wrong_explanations.C: Agreements add accountability but still expose identities the analysis never needs, so they do not minimize the data used.
wrong_explanations.D: Like coding, removing names keeps the visit linkage analysts need, though a pseudonym protects only if it means nothing to those who see it.

tips: Eliminate: B protects data only in storage, since key holders see everything, and C relies on promises instead of reducing the data shown.
Final two: A beats D because a hospital record number is a widely known identifier, while true pseudonyms need a separately protected key.
Exam cue: when a task needs linkage but not identity, look for pseudonymization with the re-identification key held apart.
